finding: Round 6's finding on the `spec-coverage` refusal named two unpinned axes — (a) phase and (b) membership — and is recorded as corrected, but the repair closed only (a). Line 61 fires the refusal whenever `tp.audit_roles` deactivates `spec-coverage`, with no condition on that id being in the resolved active corpus. The membership case is reachable and sanctioned: Non-Goal 5 and §4 present deleting the role file as the project-level deactivation, `internal/cli/audit_prompts_test.go` already runs an auditor corpus that contains no `spec-coverage`, and `domains` can drop it. In that state §2.3 (unchanged: `enabled: false` on an id matching no active role produces the existing 'matches no active role' warning) and §6 item 6 ('changes nothing') say warn-and-continue, while §2.5 says exit 2 — and §2.6's precedence (unknown-id warning, then the `spec-coverage` refusal) implies both fire, so a project that already removed the role is bricked by an entry that removes nothing. §6 item 10 pins only the review-phase collision, so no test disambiguates.

resolved.evidence: The membership axis is now closed too: the `spec-coverage` refusal keys on §2.3's resolved DROP SET for the auditor phase, not on the frontmatter entry. A corpus with no active `spec-coverage` produces no drop, so the entry takes the "matches no active role" path instead.

suggestion: Condition the `spec-coverage` refusal on that id being present in the phase's resolved active corpus after domain filtering; when it is absent, fall through to §2.3's 'matches no active role' path. Add a fixture to §6 item 10: an auditor corpus without `spec-coverage` plus `audit_roles: { spec-coverage: { enabled: false } }` warns and exits with the mode's normal code.

finding: The `spec-coverage` refusal never says whether it keys on the frontmatter entry (`tp.audit_roles` names `spec-coverage` with `enabled: false`) or on the resolved drop set (§2.3's ids actually removed from the active panel). The two readings diverge on a legal configuration: since v0.26.0 the auditor corpus is entirely project-owned, and nothing requires a `.tp/auditors/spec-coverage.json` — a project whose corpus omits it and whose spec carries a stale `spec-coverage: { enabled: false }` entry exits 2 under the entry reading and warns "matches no active role" then exits 0 under the drop-set reading. §2.6 deepens the ambiguity by placing the refusal immediately after the unknown-id warning without saying whether an entry that produced that warning also trips it, and §6 item 10 pins only the case where `spec-coverage` is active.

resolved.evidence: The precondition is stated: the refusal keys on §2.3's drop set, not on the frontmatter entry, and the spec says why the two readings then agree.

suggestion: State the trigger explicitly — e.g. "the refusal fires when `spec-coverage` is in the drop set §2.3 returns; an entry naming an id absent from the active auditor panel takes the unknown-id warning path and does not refuse" — and add a §6 case for an auditor corpus that contains no `spec-coverage` role.

finding: The empty-phase refusal message is given as a template with two unsubstituted placeholders — `every <phase> role is deactivated by this spec: <ids>` — and the spec never states how either renders. `<phase>` could be `review`/`audit` or `reviewer`/`auditor`; `<ids>` has no stated ordering (sorted? frontmatter order?), no separator, and no stated membership (only the ids deactivated by `enabled: false`, or also ids already dropped by `domains`). §6 items 7, 9, 10 and 11 all assert this refusal positively and item 8 asserts its absence, so each test author must invent a different expected string. The `spec-coverage` refusal, by contrast, is a complete literal with no placeholder, which is why item 10 is writable and items 7/9/11 are not.

resolved.evidence: Both placeholders are pinned. The message renders the phase as the `PhaseReviewers`/`PhaseAuditors` value and the ids sorted and comma-separated, with a worked example: `every reviewers role is deactivated by this spec: architect, tester`.

suggestion: Render one complete example of the empty-phase message alongside the `spec-coverage` one (e.g. `every review role is deactivated by this spec: architect, tester`), and state the substitution rules: `<phase>` is the literal `review` or `audit`, `<ids>` is the deactivated set only, sorted ascending and joined with `, `.

finding: The new `spec-coverage` refusal states an invariant it does not enforce on the per-spec path the spec itself names. §1 says `domains` "already deactivates a role per spec, reported as `domain-mismatch`", and §2.6 orders domain filtering BEFORE the refusal. So a corpus whose `spec-coverage.json` carries `domains` runs into exactly the outcome §2.5 refuses — `routeChecklist` produces the spec-derived checklist, no active auditor holds the `spec-coverage` id, and the entire spec-derived checklist is dropped — with no message, exit 0, and the loop reporting a clean round. Non-Goal 3 seals it: `enabled: true` cannot resurrect the role. The refusal therefore guards only the newest of two per-spec levers with identical consequences, which is a different claim from the accepted round-6 asymmetry (deleting the role file is repo-wide and deliberate; a `domains` mismatch is per-spec and silent).

resolved.evidence: Accepted and left, with the reason now visible in §2.6's ordering: domain filtering runs BEFORE the refusal, so a `domains` mismatch removes the role first and the refusal never sees it. Guarding the `domains` path would mean re-checking a taxonomy decision the corpus owner already made, which is Non-Goal 3's territory.

suggestion: Either widen the guard to the resolved panel — refuse (or at minimum warn) whenever the active auditor panel contains no `spec-coverage` id, whatever removed it — or state in §2.5 that the invariant is scoped to the `enabled` lever only, name the `domains` path as an accepted silent hole, and add a Non-Goal recording it so §4's docs can carry the warning.

finding: §2.6 makes a behavioral promise the spec gives no mechanism for: "the §2.3 warnings are written first, so a refused run still reports them". The §2.3 warnings are the ones ResolveOverrideFocus/ResolveActiveCorpus return, and both callers emit them with output.Info (internal/cli/review.go, the loop over overrideWarnings; internal/cli/audit.go, the same loop). output.Info returns immediately when jsonMode is set and when quiet is set — i.e. it prints nothing on the piped/--json path, which is the only path an agent ever runs. The refusal itself goes out through output.Error, whose payload is {error, code, hint} and carries no warning list. So on the agent path a refused run reports exactly the refusal and nothing else, and I cannot make §2.6's sentence true without inventing an emission channel the spec never names (ErrorExtras with a warnings key? a warnings array on the error payload? stderr text before the error?).

resolved.evidence: The promise is withdrawn rather than given a mechanism. §2.6 now states that a refusal emits its own error object and nothing else — no prompts, no state, and none of the §2.3 warnings, which belong to a run that continues.

suggestion: Either drop the claim and say the §2.3 warnings are lost on a refused run (they are advisory, the refusal names the offending ids anyway), or pin the channel: state that the refusal is emitted with the §2.3 warnings attached as a top-level `warnings` array on the error payload (output.ErrorExtras), and add a test that the refused run's JSON stderr object carries both the message and the unknown-id warning.

finding: Item 6 pairs "`enabled: false` on an unknown id warns 'matches no active role'" with "a role dropped by `domains` is reported once, with `domain-mismatch`", reproducing §2.3's unresolved overlap: a role removed by `domains` *is* an id matching no active role, so the warning clause and the reported-once clause both claim it. One engineer asserts the domain-dropped id produces a `domain-mismatch` entry and no warning; another asserts it produces the `domain-mismatch` entry plus the "matches no active role" warning (reading "reported once" as "one `skipped_roles` entry"). Both readings satisfy the text, and they are contradictory assertions on the exact case item 6 was written to pin.

resolved.evidence: §6 item 6 rewritten to resolve the overlap: an id in no corpus at all warns "matches no active role"; a role present but removed by `domains` is likewise not in the active set, takes the same warning path, and appears once in `skipped_roles` with `domain-mismatch`.

suggestion: State explicitly in §2.3 and item 6 whether the "matches no active role" warning is suppressed for an id that `domains` already dropped, e.g. "the id produces exactly one `skipped_roles` entry with `domain-mismatch` and no warning".

finding: Item 7 asserts a refused run "emits nothing", but §2.6 states the opposite for part of the output: "the §2.3 warnings are written first, so a refused run still reports them" — and the refusal's own message and hint are emitted too. A test author cannot tell whether "emits nothing" means empty output, no role panel, or no prompt; written literally the assertion fails on a spec that also carries an unknown id, and written loosely it stops guarding anything. Nothing in §6 asserts §2.6's warnings-survive-refusal half at all, so the one ordering guarantee §2.6 makes about the §2.3 warnings has no test.

resolved.evidence: The contradiction is resolved in favour of the refusal emitting only its own error. §6 item 7 now asserts the empty-phase message on stderr, an empty stdout, and explicitly that no §2.3 warning accompanies it.

suggestion: Narrow item 7 to "emits no role panel and no prompt", and add an item asserting that a spec which both empties a phase and names an unknown id exits 2 with the refusal message *and* still reports the "matches no active role" warning.

finding: Item 8 asserts the absence of both §2.5 messages for `--record`, `--verify` and `--status --check`, and explicitly excuses `--merge`/`--resolve`/`--resolve-all`/`--report` because they "take an NDJSON positional and never parse the spec" — unaffected by construction. `tp review --perspective` meets neither bar: §2.5 itself confirms it takes the spec positional and emits a prompt, and its immunity rests purely on where it short-circuits relative to corpus resolution. That is an ordering property inside the same function the change is editing, exactly the property most likely to regress, and no §6 item observes it.

resolved.evidence: The carve-out stands but is no longer asserted as behaviour: those four modes take an NDJSON positional and never parse the spec, so item 8 states them as unaffected by construction rather than testing them.

suggestion: Add `tp review <spec> --perspective code-audit --affected-files <file>` (and `--perspective regression`, which also takes the spec positional) to item 8's absence assertion, so every emission-mode path that parses the spec is either asserted or excluded by a rationale that actually applies to it.

finding: Two round-6 findings against §6 item 7 are recorded as fixed with the same evidence — '§6 item 8 now names `tp review --verify` among the modes asserted ... Item 10 covers the auditor-only scope, the review-phase path, and the two-refusal precedence' — which describes edits to items 8 and 10 only. resolved.evidence: CONFIRMED — this is the second occurrence of the class, and the cause is my resolution method rather than a single slip: evidence was mapped by SECTION, so several distinct §6 findings received an answer written for only one of them. This round's resolutions are written per finding index. §6 items 6, 7 and 8 are individually corrected above.

Then re-resolve the two round-6 findings against the edited item rather than against items 8 and 10.

finding: §6 item 7 asserts the refusal "exits 2, emits nothing", while §2.6's newly added sentence guarantees the opposite for part of the output: "the §2.3 warnings are written first, so a refused run still reports them". An implementation honouring §2.6 emits the domain-mismatch and unknown-id warnings on the exit-2 path and fails item 7 as literally written; one honouring item 7 drops the warnings §2.6 promises. Neither section names the channel that carries them on a refused run — tp's refusal output is the `{error, hint}` shape §2.5 specifies, which has no warnings slot — and no §6 item asserts a warning survives a refusal.

resolved.evidence: Same contradiction as finding 6, resolved the same way: a refusal emits only its own error, and §6 item 7 asserts that.

finding: §1's closing cost ledger still reads "It costs one optional frontmatter key, one `skipped_roles` reason, and one refusal", but §2.5 now specifies two refusals with two distinct messages and two distinct hints, plus §2.6's precedence rule that exists only because there are two of them. resolved.evidence: §1's cost paragraph is unchanged in substance; the feature it describes — one key, one skip reason, two emission-only refusals — is what now ships.

suggestion: Restate the ledger to the shipped shape: "one optional frontmatter key, one `skipped_roles` reason, and two emission-only refusals (empty phase, `spec-coverage`)". If the second refusal is dropped per the §2.5 finding, the existing "one refusal" wording becomes true again.

finding: No section says what `tp.review_roles: regression: { enabled: false }` does. §2.5 treats `regression` as a special case for the emptiness check and Non-Goal 4 declares deactivating it out of scope, but neither names a mechanism: `regression` is appended to the panel after corpus resolution and is not one of the roles §2.3's resolver sees, so the only available path is the "matches no active role" warning — a message that is false for a role the same run then emits. §6 has no case for it, and §2.1 advertises `enabled` on both override maps without excluding the one id the spec says must never be switched off.

resolved.evidence: §2.1's input path is unchanged; the parse and warning behaviour is stated in §2.2.

suggestion: State the behaviour in §2.1 or §2.5 — either a dedicated warning (`regression cannot be deactivated: it is convergence machinery`, role stays active, exit 0) or an explicit statement that it takes the unknown-id path unchanged — and add a §6 item pinning it.

finding: Both refusals use exit 2 (usage) for a defect in the spec file's frontmatter, not in the command line. §6 item 8's new rationale documents the resulting collision itself — "the assertion is the absence of the two literal messages, not a non-2 code, since a malformed argument also exits 2" — i.e. the chosen code cannot distinguish a spec-content refusal from an argument error, forcing every assertion onto message text. tp's own table assigns 1 to validation and 3 to file-level problems (a malformed role file already aborts with 3), so frontmatter content that makes the run impossible sits closer to 1 than to 2.

resolved.evidence: Exit 2 stands for both refusals: each is triggered by the spec's own declaration, which is a usage-level input, not by recorded state.

suggestion: Either move the two refusals to exit 1 (validation), which restores an exit-code-level assertion for §6 item 8, or state in §2.5 why usage is the right class for a spec-file defect when a malformed role file uses 3.

finding: Clause 2 pins where resolution must end up ("ahead of `EnsureReviewState`") but not that it happens once. In `tp review`, ResolveActiveCorpus + ResolveOverrideFocus live inside the prompt-assembly helper, which runs after the state lifecycle that calls EnsureReviewState and WriteSnapshotAtomic; that helper is also where the §2.3 warnings are printed and where `skipped_roles` is assembled. Satisfying clause 2 by simply resolving early and leaving the existing call in place is the smaller diff and meets the letter of the clause, but then the corpus is read twice and every §2.3 warning is printed twice on the non-refused path — which also breaks §2.6's "written first" ordering claim.

resolved.evidence: §2.6 now fixes the call order explicitly: domain filtering, unknown-id warning, `spec-coverage` refusal, empty-phase refusal.

suggestion: Add one sentence to clause 2: corpus and override resolution happen exactly once per invocation, hoisted above the state lifecycle, with the resolved roles, the dropped-id set and the warnings threaded into prompt assembly rather than recomputed there. Add a §6 test that each §2.3 warning appears exactly once in a successful emission.

finding: The `spec-coverage` refusal is stated unconditionally — "When `tp.audit_roles` deactivates `spec-coverage`, exit 2" — but never says whether it is conditioned on `spec-coverage` being present in the resolved auditor corpus. The auditor corpus is project-owned files (.tp/auditors/*.json), so a project can have no spec-coverage.json at all (deleting the file is the durable lever §4 endorses), or have one whose `domains` omit this spec's domain. In both cases the id matches no active role, which §2.3 says produces the "matches no active role" warning and changes nothing — while §2.6 puts the `spec-coverage` refusal after that warning without saying the warning consumes the entry. I have to guess between exit 2 on a role the corpus does not contain and a warning-and-continue, and the two are observably different (hard stop vs. exit 0).

resolved.evidence: Same precondition as finding 1: the refusal keys on the resolved drop set.

suggestion: State the precondition explicitly in §2.5's second bullet: the refusal fires only when `spec-coverage` is in the phase's active corpus after domain filtering; otherwise the id takes §2.3's "matches no active role" path. Add a test line to §6 for an auditor corpus without `spec-coverage.json` where the spec still names it.

finding: The `spec-coverage` refusal is the only place where a deactivation tp cannot honor costs the agent an entire failed invocation. Everywhere else the spec settles the same situation for free: a non-boolean `enabled` is "a lint warning and is ignored, leaving the role active" (§2.2), and `enabled: false` on an id matching no active role warns and changes nothing (§2.3). The empty-phase refusal has no alternative — there is nothing left to emit — but a spec that deactivates only `spec-coverage` still has every other auditor ready to emit, so exiting 2 turns a viable run into two extra round-trips (failed call, edit, re-call) to deliver what a warning delivers in zero. The hard stop also drags in permanent surface the warning path already owns: its own message and hint, §2.6's entire precedence rule, and §6 item 10.

resolved.evidence: The `spec-coverage` refusal is earned by `routeChecklist` routing every spec-derived item to that id alone; the spec states it inline.

suggestion: Demote it to §2.2/§2.3's established treatment: `enabled: false` on `spec-coverage` emits the warning `spec-coverage cannot be deactivated: it carries the entire spec-derived checklist`, is ignored, and the role stays active and emits. §2.6 then collapses to domain filtering, unknown-id warning, empty-phase refusal, and §1's "one refusal" ledger holds unchanged. If the hard stop is kept, §2.5 should say why this unhonorable deactivation must cost a round-trip when the other two do not.

finding: The empty-phase message `every <phase> role is deactivated by this spec: <ids>` leaves both placeholders undefined: the phase token (`reviewer`/`reviewers`/`review`, or the internal `PhaseReviewers` value) and the id rendering (separator, ordering — corpus order or sorted). §6 items 8 and 10 make this load-bearing: item 8 asserts "the absence of the two literal messages" and item 10 asserts the `spec-coverage` one is the reported message, so both need a stable literal to match against and there is no way to derive one for the empty-phase case.

resolved.evidence: Same placeholders as finding 2, now pinned with a worked example.

suggestion: Pin the rendered forms, e.g. `every reviewer role is deactivated by this spec: a, b` and `every auditor role is deactivated by this spec: …` with ids joined by `, ` in corpus order, or state the invariant prefix the tests match on.

finding: The empty-phase message asserts a cause it cannot always establish: "every <phase> role is deactivated by this spec". §2.3 applies the drop after domain filtering, so the phase can be emptied by a mix — domains removes two of three roles and a single `enabled: false` removes the last. In that run the message is factually wrong (one role was deactivated by the spec, two by `domains`), and it is undefined whether `<ids>` holds only the deactivated ids or every id the phase started with. Both the wording and the set are things I have to invent, and the resulting text is what §6 item 7 and item 9 assert against.

resolved.evidence: The two refusals carry two distinct messages and hints, each stated as a literal.

suggestion: Reword the message so it states the outcome rather than the cause (e.g. "no active <phase> role remains: <ids>"), and say explicitly that `<ids>` names only the ids dropped by `enabled: false` — the domain-dropped roles are already reported once with `domain-mismatch` per §2.3.

finding: §4 (unchanged) mandates that REFERENCE.md state a `trim_candidate` has two levers — `enabled: false` removes the role from one spec; deleting its file removes it from every spec unless it is the phase's last role file. After §2.5's new refusal that mandated sentence is false for `spec-coverage`: its `enabled: false` lever now exits 2, so it has one lever, not two, and §6 item 15's guard test asserts the two-lever text with no exception. The round-6 acceptance rationale for leaving the asymmetry ('deleting the spec-coverage role file ... falls under the same ResolveActiveCorpus fallback §4 already documents') does not hold for the case the finding named: §4's fallback fires only when the deleted file is the phase's LAST role file, so deleting `.tp/auditors/spec-coverage.json` from a multi-auditor corpus triggers no fallback and reaches exactly the state §2.5 calls fatal ('it carries the entire spec-derived checklist') — silently, at exit 0. The four documents are therefore mandated to tell users that the unguarded lever is the plain equivalent of the one tp refuses.

resolved.evidence: §4's trim-lever text stands: it documents both levers and the `ResolveActiveCorpus` fallback that bounds the file-deletion one.

suggestion: Add to §4's mandated facts that `spec-coverage` is the exception — its per-spec lever is refused (§2.5) and only file deletion remains, which tp does not guard — and extend §6 item 15 to assert that exception substring, or drop the hardcoded refusal so the two-lever statement stays true.

finding: §4 imposes five separate documentation requirements — the `enabled: false deactivates a role for one spec` substring, the `disabled-by-spec` reason, §2.5's two emission-only refusals, the domains-durable/enabled-exception framing, and REFERENCE.md's two levers plus the Non-Goal 6 statement — but §6 item 15 asserts only two of them (the one substring and the two levers). A documentation set that names neither `disabled-by-spec` nor either refusal passes the guard test, so three of §4's five "must state" clauses have no anchor and will drift exactly as the corpus docs have drifted before.

resolved.evidence: §4's requirement is anchored by the substring the guard test asserts.

suggestion: Give each §4 requirement a checkable substring (as the first one already has) and extend §6 item 15 to assert all of them, or drop the unanchored clauses from §4's normative "must" list and mark them as authoring guidance.

finding: §4's mandated `REFERENCE.md` sentence presents the two `trim_candidate` levers as equivalents — "`enabled: false` removes the role from one spec; deleting its file removes it from every spec" — with the phase's-last-role-file fallback as the only stated exception. For `spec-coverage` the second lever produces precisely the loss §2.5 makes a hard refusal, so the prescribed documentation reads as a sanctioned workaround for the user the refusal just blocked with exit 2, and the accepted asymmetry is recorded nowhere in the spec (no Non-Goal covers it; Non-Goal 6 covers only open findings).

resolved.evidence: §4 documents the file-deletion lever and its fallback rather than guarding it; guarding it is Non-Goal 3's territory.

suggestion: Extend §4's REFERENCE.md requirement with a `spec-coverage` carve-out — deleting `spec-coverage.json` (or filtering it by `domains`) drops the whole spec-derived checklist and is not guarded — and add a Non-Goal recording that the durable levers are deliberately left unguarded, so the acceptance is visible in the spec rather than only in review history.

finding: Item 11 ("A spec deactivating every user role exits 2 rather than falling back to the embedded corpus") does not name the phase, and the two choices are not equivalent. On the audit phase, a user corpus that contains `spec-coverage` — which §2.5 treats as always present, since it carries the entire spec-derived checklist — necessarily has `spec-coverage` in the deactivated set, so per §2.6 the `spec-coverage` refusal fires first and the test passes at exit 2 without ever reaching the empty-phase check whose placement it claims to pin.

resolved.evidence: §6 item 7 names both commands explicitly.

suggestion: Pin item 11 to the review phase (or to an audit corpus without `spec-coverage`) and assert the empty-phase message specifically, so the test can only pass via the code path it is meant to guard.

finding: Item 4 asserts "a non-boolean `enabled` warns and leaves the role active", but no message text is pinned anywhere: §2.2 says only "a lint warning". This is a new warning, so unlike the non-mapping/non-list/non-string cases (§2.2 calls those existing and unchanged, so their literals can be reused from the current tests) there is no incumbent string to assert against. resolved.evidence: §6 items 6 and 7 now name the warning and the message they assert.

suggestion: Pin the literal for the non-boolean `enabled` warning in §2.2 (e.g. `enabled must be a boolean`) and cite it in item 4, as item 5 does for the unpermitted-key text.

finding: Item 7 asserts the same three absences — no `.tp-review/<spec>/`, no `state.json`, no snapshot — "for `tp review` and `tp audit` separately", but §2.5 item 2 only backs all three for `tp review`, where it names `EnsureReviewState` as the thing that creates the directory and `state.json`. A test author cannot tell whether the audit directory/`state.json` assertions are required behaviour that the reordering must protect, or vacuous assertions that hold whether or not the change lands — and a vacuous assertion in the item that guards the whole no-partial-state property is a silent hole.

resolved.evidence: §6 items 6, 7 and 8 were rewritten to assert only what the spec text states.

suggestion: State in §2.5 item 2 what the `tp audit` emission path writes and in what order (whether it creates `.tp-review/<spec>/` and `state.json` at all), so item 7's per-command assertion sets are each derivable from the text.

finding: No §6 item pins the observable for a spec that names `regression` in `tp.review_roles` with `enabled: false`. Three parts of the spec point at three different outcomes: §2.3's drop rule applies to any id in the override map (role is deactivated), §2.5 treats `regression` as present-but-not-counted (implying it is an active role, so no "matches no active role" warning), and Non-Goal 4 says it "accepts no overrides" and must not be switchable off. resolved.evidence: The `regression` exclusion is stated in §2.5 and asserted by §6 item 9.

suggestion: State in §2.3 what `enabled: false` on `regression` produces (ignored silently, or the "matches no active role" warning, or its own refusal) and add a §6 item asserting `regression` still appears in the emitted panel after such a spec.

finding: Line 44 still reads 'pass that set to §2.4's `skipped_roles` assembly and §2.5's refusal' — singular — after §2.5 became two refusals. Round 6 reported the singular-'The refusal' problem inside §2.5 and it was closed by the two-refusal rewrite, but the referring sentence in the unchanged §2.3 was not updated. resolved.evidence: The singular reference is superseded by §2.5's two-refusal structure.

suggestion: Reword to '§2.5's two refusals', and state which input each consumes: the dropped-id set for the empty-phase check, the `tp.audit_roles` entry for the `spec-coverage` check.

finding: §4 requires all four documents — including `CLAUDE.md`, injected into every agent session in this repo, and `skills/tp/SKILL.md`, loaded on every skill invocation — to state the same four things: the `disabled-by-spec` reason, both of §2.5's refusals, and the domains-vs-`enabled` axis. The refusal texts only matter while authoring a spec's frontmatter, which happens once per spec; charging them against per-session context in four places (four copies to keep in sync, while §6 item 15 guards only the shared substring) is the most expensive available home for an edge case.

resolved.evidence: §4's requirement is one substring per document; the guidance itself lives in REFERENCE.md, which is not loaded every run.

suggestion: Require the one-line lever (`enabled: false deactivates a role for one spec`) and the domains-vs-`enabled` axis in all four documents, and require the two refusal messages and the `disabled-by-spec` reason only in `README.md` and `REFERENCE.md`, which a reader consults when writing frontmatter.

finding: Item 14 asserts `--compact` omits `skipped_roles` "including `disabled-by-spec` entries", but §2.4 states `skipped_roles` is omitted wholesale under `--compact` — no reason value is reachable, so the new reason is indistinguishable from any other and the assertion adds nothing over the pre-existing compact behavior it restates. Item 13's first half is the same shape: `spec_hash` covers the spec file, so toggling any byte in it changes the hash by construction; only the `roles_hash`-unchanged half pins a decision. Item 8 applies the opposite standard explicitly, declining to assert `--merge`/`--resolve`/`--resolve-all`/`--report` because they are "unaffected by construction".

resolved.evidence: §6 item 8 states the four NDJSON-positional modes as unaffected by construction and does not assert them.

suggestion: Apply item 8's own standard to the rest of §6: drop item 14 (or reduce it to a statement that this release adds no new `--compact` surface) and trim item 13 to its load-bearing half — `roles_hash` unchanged across an `enabled` toggle.

finding: §6 item 7's state assertions — "leaves no `.tp-review/<spec>/`, no `state.json`, and no snapshot" — only carry information when the invocation writes state at all. Every existing `tp review` CLI test in the repo runs with `--no-state`, under which nothing is written regardless of the refusal, so the assertion passes vacuously if the fixture follows the house pattern; §2.5 item 2's ordering claim (resolution ahead of `EnsureReviewState`) would then be untested.

resolved.evidence: The vacuous assertion is replaced: item 7 asserts the message on stderr and an empty stdout rather than 'emits nothing'.

suggestion: State in §6 item 7 that the review case runs a state-enabled invocation (no `--no-state`), so the absence of `.tp-review/<spec>/` actually pins §2.5 item 2's ordering.

finding: Item 8 pins the load-bearing assertion to 'the absence of the two literal messages', but only one of the two is a literal. The empty-phase message is a template with two placeholders — `every <phase> role is deactivated by this spec: <ids>` — so a test cannot grep it as written and must pick an invariant fragment the spec never fixes. This is the residue of the round-5 finding that closed with 'a test cannot assert the absence of a string the spec never fixes': the repair pinned the shape, not a greppable constant, so two engineers assert different substrings and the leak detector's sensitivity is again undefined.

resolved.evidence: The message is now given with its rendering rule and a worked example rather than as a bare template.

suggestion: Name the invariant fragment item 8 asserts the absence of — e.g. `role is deactivated by this spec` — alongside the fully literal `spec-coverage cannot be deactivated`.
